sentences.text: In order to do the things an animal needs to do, eat, drink, breathe, make babies,
stuff needs to come into our bodies, and other stuff needs to leave. That's why we
animals have holes. But exactly how many holes those jobs require and which job each hole
does turns out to be wildly different from one animal to the next. Hi, I'm David
and this is Minute Earth. In us humans, food enters our body through our mouths and
leaves as poop through our butts. In one hole, out the other. It makes sense to
us, but not every animal does it that way. The lion's mane jellyfish, for instance, uses
only one hole for the same process. Food goes in and waste comes out the same
way. It might seem weird and kind of gross with the stuff coming in and the
stuff going out to share one hole. But this is exactly how humans are set up
when it comes to breathing. Oxygen enters our body via one hole. For the purposes of
this video, we're going to call our nose and mouth a single hole since they're connected and
serve the same purpose. And the waste from breathing, carbon dioxide, leaves through the very same
hole, which is also the same hole we eat through since our respiratory system and digestive
system share the same pipes,
at least for a while. Which again probably seems totally normal, but that isn't how all animals
do it. Beluga whales, for example, eat through one hole and breathe through an entirely different
one. In other words, there's no normal number or configuration of holes in the animal kingdom.
Species are all over the map. So, we decided to literally map out the various holes
and pathways through which stuff travels in and out of all kinds of animals.
Obviously, we had to put some boundaries around what counts as a hole. Otherwise, this would
turn into a Vsauce video. For our purposes, a hole is an opening in the body
that facilitates the essential functions of life on Earth: energy, waste, and reproduction.
So, ears and belly buttons don't count, nor do nipples or sweat glands. The opening also
has to be somewhat sizable compared to the animal's body. So, the dozens of tiny pores
and ducts and spiracles that some animals drink and breathe through don't count. We'll treat anything
passing through those as just passing through the body's surface.
Let's see some maps, shall we? The lion's main jellyfish, the one that eats and poops
through the same hole, has in fact just that single hole through which it also pumps
out sperm or eggs. All of its other essential functions happen through its body's surface.
A chicken though has two holes. It eats, drinks, and breathes through one hole, its mouth.
At the other end, it has a hole called the cloa through which it pees, poops,
takes in sperm, and lays eggs. A clamor
also has two holes, a mouth it eats through, and a butt it poops through. But
that's all its holes do. It breathes in and out through its skin, drinks and pees
through its skin, and even releases its eggs or sperm through its skin.
Now, let's look at some three-holeers.
An emperor scorpion has a mouth hole for eating and drinking, and a butthole next to
its stinger for peeing and pooping. It's also got a genital hole under its back legs
used for both mating and in the females, birth, and it breathes in and out through
spiracles throughout its body. A sea cucumber also has a similar three-hole setup, except that it
doesn't really need to drink, at least not in the usual sense of the word, and
it pees through its body wall. And oh yeah, it also breathes in and out through
its butt. That's right, it breathes in and out through its butt. Another three-holeer is a
human. Well, a human male to be specific. Our mouth hole is used for eating and
drinking and breathing in and out. At the other end, instead of routing everything else out
through a single all-purpose cloica, the way a chicken does, male humans split that exit in
two, adding a third hole, the urethra, where urine and sperm come out. Human females, though,
actually have four holes. Most holes are the same as the males, eating, drinking, and breathing
through the mouth, pooping through the butt. The difference is that a female's urethra, handles only
peeing, while a separate hole, the vagina,
handles the ins and outs of reproduction.
Female butterflies also have four holes, but with a different arrangement of functions. Peeing is bundled
up with pooping, but reproduction
split up. A butterfly has one hole to receive sperm during mating and a totally separate
hole through which it lays its eggs, and it breeds in and out through spiracles on
its body. Then there's a female Nile tilapia.
Like other fish, it uses two separate holes for breathing. Its mouth and its operculum, which
covers the gills. And like other freshwater fish, it doesn't really drink much. But unlike lots
of other fish, it's got totally separate holes for pooping, peeing, and laying eggs. It's a
rare fiveholer.
We are so enamored with the incredible diversity of holes and bodily functions across the animal
kingdom that we made a whole poster about it. But before we tell you how to
get it, we have one final configuration
to discuss.
Let's talk tapeworms.
A tapeworm lives its entire life inside another animal's gut, absorbing nutrients and releasing waste straight
through its skin. No food hole, no poop hole, no breath hole, no pee hole. It
doesn't even need a hole to reproduce. It just grows already fertilized eggpacked body segments which
eventually break off. It's got no holes at all. Which on a planet full of one-hole
jellyfish,
three whole sea cucumbers,
and four whole butterflies
is just one more way to do it. And that's more or less the whole story.

configurations,
all of which are drawn like old school subway maps by our amazing illustrators. Whether it's

conversation starter. And you can get it right now by clicking on the link in the
